abstract: Biofilms form persistent surface-associated communities across natural, industrial, and biomedical environments and cause significant socioeconomic distress, yet their controlled removal remains challenging, especially in wet and underwater conditions. Inspired by barnacle adhesives that clear underlying biomass before their permanent attachment, here we introduce adhesive peeling as a readily adoptable, practical strategy for controlled removal and characterization of biofilms underwater. Using underwater adhesives, force-controlled contact peeling, and in situ confocal microscopy, we show that bacterial biofilms can be transferred from submerged surfaces to an adhesive, with removal reaching ~ 82%. Additionally, with a mechano-interfacial map that combines underwater biofilm-adhesive work of adhesion and biofilm-adhesive mechanical mismatch, we found three distinct species-dependent adhesive peeling mechanisms: (i) E. coli peeling is dominated by favorable interfacial interactions and is insensitive to adhesive mechanics, (ii) S. aureus peeling requires a balance between interfacial affinity and mechanical response, and (iii) P. aeruginosa peeling is insensitive to adhesive identity, consistent with cohesion-limited failure within the biofilm. These results establish adhesive peeling as a methodology for both removing biofilms and identifying the dominant failure pathway within submerged adhesive-biofilm-substrate-water interfaces, providing a physical basis for understanding how living biofilms contact, adhere, and fail against non-living materials across healthcare, transportation, and industrial systems where persistent biofouling carries substantial human and economic costs.
